prohibited_recommendations: Do not give IV thrombolysis: the standard window has passed (10 hours 45 minutes from last known well), FLAIR is positive, and a 3-week-old oesophagogastric anastomosis after resection of a gastrointestinal malignancy makes systemic thrombolysis high risk.
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or labs in a stroke alert presentation.

Do not start or restart antihypertensive treatment in the first 48 to 72 hours for blood pressure below 220/120 mmHg in a patient who receives neither IV thrombolysis nor thrombectomy and has no comorbid indication; it does not prevent death or dependency (AHA/ASA 2026, COR 3: No Benefit).
Do not start full-dose anticoagulation before follow-up imaging excludes haemorrhagic transformation or before day 6 to 7 for this large infarct, and do not bridge with heparin.
Do not perform transoesophageal echocardiography early after oesophagectomy: probe passage risks the cervical anastomosis, and TEE would not change management.
Do not withhold anticoagulation indefinitely because of the recent surgery: recurrence risk in atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation is high; agree a start date with the surgical team.
Do not attribute the new confusion and left-sided inattention to postoperative delirium without brain imaging.
required_recommendations: Establish last known well (22:00, 10 hours 45 minutes before arrival) and the NIHSS (8).

IV thrombolysis: do not give. The standard window has passed (10 hours 45 minutes from last known well); FLAIR is positive, so the DWI-FLAIR limb is closed; the perfusion limb (wake-up stroke within 9 hours of the sleep midpoint, about 02:45, 6 hours before arrival, in a patient not eligible for thrombectomy) is not pursued because a 3-week-old oesophagogastric anastomosis after resection of a gastrointestinal malignancy makes systemic thrombolysis high risk. Thrombectomy: not indicated; an isolated P2 occlusion is a medium vessel occlusion with no graded thrombectomy indication, and NIHSS 8 does not meet the basilar criteria; recent surgery would not in itself have been a contraindication to thrombectomy.
Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours.
Screen swallowing before any oral intake or oral medicine, given the aspiration pneumonia after his oesophagectomy.

Control the ventricular rate (104 bpm on arrival on metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily) by up-titrating metoprolol cautiously, avoiding hypotension; rapid atrial fibrillation lowers cardiac output and perfusion of the ischaemic territory.

Start apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc 5: hypertension, age 65 to 74, diabetes, stroke 2; HAS-BLED 3: stroke, anaemia as bleeding predisposition, age over 65) on day 6 to 7 once follow-up imaging excludes haemorrhagic transformation (a 5 cm infarct spanning the PCA cortical territory and the MCA border zone; the later ELAN start also suits the 3-week-old anastomosis), with the start date agreed with the surgical team; stop prophylactic enoxaparin when apixaban starts and do not bridge with therapeutic heparin.
Continue prophylactic-dose enoxaparin for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis (recent surgery, cancer, reduced mobility) until apixaban starts.

Use transthoracic echocardiography for the cardiac evaluation and defer TEE: probe passage early after oesophagectomy risks the anastomosis, and TEE would not change management because atrial fibrillation already indicates anticoagulation.
Intensify atorvastatin to 80 mg (LDL 128 mg/dL on 40 mg, with diabetes and carotid and basilar plaque); target LDL below 70 mg/dL.

Surgery 21 days ago is a week beyond the 14-day interval of the recent-major-surgery rule; what weighs against thrombolysis is the fresh anastomosis after gastrointestinal cancer surgery, not that rule.
An isolated P2 occlusion is a medium vessel occlusion with no graded thrombectomy indication (ESCAPE-MeVO and DISTAL showed no benefit), and NIHSS 8 does not meet the basilar criteria.

The right PCA has a fetal-type origin from the right ICA: a left atrial embolus reached it through the anterior circulation, and the combined PCA and posterior MCA border-zone infarct extending into the posterior corona radiata explains the mild left hemiparesis beside the hemianopia, neglect and sensory loss.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Robert Kessler is a 67-year-old right-handed man with a history of distal esophageal adenocarcinoma (status post neoadjuvant chemotherapy and en bloc esophagectomy three weeks ago), atrial fibrillation (anticoagulation discontinued perioperatively and not restarted), hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia, who was transferred emergently from the acute rehabilitation unit after nursing staff noted new neurological deficits during the routine 07:00 morning assessment. The patient had been admitted to the rehabilitation facility two days ago following a prolonged postoperative hospital course complicated by a brief episode of aspiration pneumonia that has since resolved. On the morning of transfer, the rehabilitation nurse noticed the patient was having difficulty navigating the left side of his breakfast tray and repeatedly bumped into the doorframe on his left side when attempting to walk to the bathroom. When questioned, the patient seemed confused and was slow to respond, though he had been alert and conversant the evening prior. The last documented neurological check at 22:00 the night before was unremarkable; he settled to sleep at about 22:30, and the overnight nursing notes documented that he slept through the night without any reported events. His wife, who was visiting in the morning, confirmed that he had been at his postoperative baseline the previous evening, engaging in conversation and watching television without difficulty. She noted that when she arrived at 07:30 this morning, he appeared confused, was not tracking objects to his left, and had difficulty using his left hand to hold his coffee cup. There was no report of headache, seizure activity, nausea, vomiting, or fever. Given his history of esophageal cancer, the rehabilitation team was concerned about possible brain metastasis versus a new stroke, particularly in light of his discontinued anticoagulation, and activated a stroke alert for emergent transfer to the emergency department. He arrived in the ED at 08:45. His last known well time is 22:00 the night before, 10 hours 45 minutes before arrival.
